affected_ids: 3.2 claim "A supply contraction with demand unchanged raises equilibrium price…"
issues.finding: A leftward shift of supply is called a "contraction" ("can contract bread supply", "contracted supply curve S2", "supply contracts left", "supply contraction"). In the convention NSSCO inherits, contraction/extension mean movements ALONG a curve; a shift is an increase/decrease. The notes elsewhere carefully separate movements from shifts, so this word undermines their own distinction.
issues.evidence: 3.2-014-APP answer "…less is offered at each price and supply contracts left." Examiner material for this subject uses "decrease in supply" for a leftward shift and "shift S to S1".
issues.educational_consequence: Learners may write "contraction of supply" for a shift, or misread an exam question that uses "contraction" for a movement along the curve, and lose the shift/movement mark.
issues.recommended_repair: Replace with "decrease in supply (leftward shift)" in all listed blocks, items and the claim text. Optionally add one sentence in B-6145-3.2-002/003 that extension/contraction describe movements along a curve. Revise and restamp the claim. The wording comes from the planning performance spec, but fixing the learner text needs no plan rebuild.

issues.finding: The central-bank block describes the bank's functions only vaguely ("can have responsibilities relating to currency, the government's banking arrangements, banks' settlement needs"). It never plainly teaches the functions examined in this subject: issuing notes and coins, banker to the government, banker/lender of last resort to commercial banks, managing foreign reserves, and conducting monetary policy (interest rates). No item asks the learner to identify or describe them.
issues.evidence: The 2021, 2023 and 2024 examiner reports ask learners to list or describe central-bank functions, and the 2024 report says learners listed functions but failed to describe them. The notes give learners neither the list nor a model description.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner using only the notes would lose most marks on a common "List/Describe the functions of a central bank" question.
issues.recommended_repair: In B-6145-2.3-009, add a short paragraph naming each standard function, with a one-sentence description of how it works. Keep the Namibia peg constraint and avoid current figures. Point one existing FEATURE answer (for example 2.3-015, or P01 part 4) at two named functions, without changing slot labels. Add a supporting claim or revise an existing one, then restamp.

issues.finding: Sole-proprietor risk is described ("personal resources at risk under the applicable rules") but the standard term "unlimited liability" never appears, although "limited liability" is taught.
issues.educational_consequence: Learners may not connect the idea to the term used in exam wording and mark schemes.
issues.recommended_repair: Name it once: "this is usually called unlimited liability", keeping the existing caution about legal detail.

issues.finding: (a) The recorded deviation replaced "depreciation" with "capital-consumption allowance" to satisfy a currency-condition check. The word learners will meet in gross/net national-accounts questions now never appears in 7.3. (b) The 1-mark learner definitions end with hedges ("under the stated convention", "with the accounting measure specified") that are not usable exam answers.
issues.educational_consequence: A minor loss of recognition marks and odd model definitions.
issues.recommended_repair: Add a parenthetical gloss such as "capital consumption (the wearing out of capital, often called depreciation)". If C-check matching blocks this, record it as a tool limitation rather than dropping the term. Shorten the DEF answers, e.g. "GDP adjusted by net factor income from abroad".

issues.finding: These items reuse generic rubric text (e.g. "Context (1): use the stated comparison. Reason/conclusion (1): the explained consequence follows from the supplied condition") instead of naming the creditable points. The canonical answers themselves are specific and correct.
issues.educational_consequence: Weaker self-marking: learners cannot see which exact point earns each mark.
issues.recommended_repair: Generate item-specific marking guidance from each canonical answer, as already done in 1.x–3.x and 5.1–5.3. Optional but worthwhile.

issues.finding: After teaching maximum and minimum prices, the block says "topic 6.3 examines reasons and methods of government intervention". 6.3 covers production controls and protection, not price controls, so a learner following the link for price-control evaluation finds nothing.
issues.recommended_repair: Reword so it does not imply 6.3 develops price controls (e.g. "topic 6.3 examines other reasons and methods of intervention in business").

issues.finding: The prompt already says "a rise in long-run average cost", so the learner only has to restate a definition. The planned confusion between economies and diseconomies (MIS-6145-007) is not really tested.
issues.recommended_repair: Give a scenario without the label (e.g. expansion where coordination delays raise unit cost from N$8 to N$11) and ask why calling it an economy of scale is wrong.

issues.finding: The 1-mark answer to "Define a fertility rate" describes two measures at once. It is correct but not a usable one-line definition.
issues.recommended_repair: Use a single definition (e.g. "the average number of births per woman, or births per thousand women of child-bearing age in a year") and keep the GFR/TFR distinction in the notes.
